title: Put yourself in their place
hookLine: all fear punishment and love life; put yourself in their place, and don't harm (Dhammapada 129–130)
tomorrow: can a whole religion fit into three short lines?

lines: A FIGHT OVER THE BETTER ROOM.
cards: Roommates fight over the better room. In the Dhammapada's commentary, it's monks. A group of seventeen young monks has settled into a lodging.
A group of six arrives and orders them out. The young ones refuse. So the six start hitting them, and the seventeen cry out loud enough to be heard across the monastery.
What makes the Buddha step in isn't the noise. It's a thought about fear.

teach.h: A RULE: NO MONK STRIKES ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Buddha asks what's happening, and he's told. He lays down a training rule: a monk must not strike another monk. Then he gives the reason, and the reason is the verse.

In Max Müller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." The next verse says the same with life: all love it.
In Pali, the key phrase is attanam upamam katva: making yourself the comparison. You know what a blow feels like. So does everyone.
So does every creature that can flinch.
Buddhists hear in this the reasoning behind the first of the five precepts: to refrain from taking life. Monks and lay Buddhists alike recite it. It isn't only a rule handed down.

It comes with its own test, one anyone can run: put yourself in their place, then decide. And the precept reaches past people, to animals and insects: anything that fears the stick is in the comparison.
A child can understand it. That's the point. You don't need a doctrine to know a creature is afraid.

how: The first of the five precepts that lay Buddhists recite is to refrain from taking life; monks and nuns keep it as part of a longer code, and Buddhist teachers often explain it with Dhammapada 129–130.

games.q: what does “put yourself in their place” mean?
o: imagining another's fear before you do any harm
trading places with someone for a whole day
asking someone else to decide for you

games.q: the fight and the rule: tap the pairs.
p: the young monks who cried out
a monk must not strike another

s: the first precept is only for monks and nuns
lay Buddhists take it too: to refrain from taking life.
the verse gives a reason for not harming, not just a command
all tremble at punishment; remember that you are like unto them.
the verse's only reason for not harming is to avoid bad luck yourself
the verse's reason is the other's fear: all tremble at the rod, so put yourself in their place.

games.q: you're the Buddha. two groups of monks have come to blows over a room. you make a rule against striking. what reason do you give?
o: fighting brings shame on the community in front of the town.
everyone trembles at punishment; make yourself the comparison.
the room belongs to whoever arrived first, so the six were wrong.
games.why: the reason is the verse: all fear the rod and love life. put yourself in their place, and don't harm.

practice: Look at one living thing near you: a plant, a bird at the window, a pet, an insect on the wall, the person across the room. Let yourself picture what it fears, a shadow, a loud noise, being hurt.
Then stay with it quietly, as one more creature that trembles and loves being alive.

wordCard.voice: Put yourself in their place: the Buddha's test before any harm. All tremble at the rod; all love life; make yourself the comparison.

orig.note: Pali, in roman letters with marks: making oneself the comparison, the key phrase of verses 129 and 130.

carryVoice: For the road: in their place, before anything else. That's day eight with the verses.

sources.q: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 130 (all love life; the same reasoning)
Dhammapada Commentary on verses 129–130: the group of six monks and the group of seventeen; the Buddha lays down a rule against striking (cf. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, 1921)
the five precepts: the first, to refrain from taking life (e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 8.39)
